verses.text: After Hezekiah had done all this faithfully, King Sennacherib of Assyria invaded Judah. He camped outside the fortified cities, planning to take them for himself.
Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had arrived and was coming for Jerusalem.
He got together with his officials and warriors to figure out how to cut off the springs outside the city, and they helped him do it.
A crowd showed up and blocked all the springs and the stream that ran through the land. “Why let the kings of Assyria come here and find water everywhere?” they said.
Hezekiah took courage. He rebuilt every broken stretch of wall up to the towers, put up another wall outside it, and reinforced the Millo in David’s city. He also made loads of weapons and shields.
He put military commanders in charge of the people, called everyone together in the square by the city gate, and gave them this encouragement:
“Stand strong and be brave. Don’t let the king of Assyria or the huge crowd with him scare you or shake you. Someone greater is with us than with him.
All he’s got is human strength. We’ve got the LORD our God with us to help us and fight our battles.” The people took heart from what Hezekiah, king of Judah, said.

Later, while King Sennacherib of Assyria and his whole army were attacking Lachish, he sent officials to Jerusalem with a message for King Hezekiah of Judah and all the people of Judah gathered there.
“This is what Sennacherib, king of Assyria, says: Who are you counting on while you sit in Jerusalem under siege?
Isn’t Hezekiah talking you into dying of hunger and thirst when he says, ‘The LORD our God will rescue us from the king of Assyria’?
Isn’t Hezekiah the same man who took away your God’s high places and altars and told Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You’re to worship at one altar and burn incense on it’?
Don’t you know what my ancestors and I did to the peoples of those lands? Could any of their gods save their land from me?
Of all the gods of the nations my ancestors wiped out, which one could save its people from me? What makes you think your God can save you from me?

So don’t let Hezekiah fool you or talk you into this. Don’t believe him. No god of any nation or kingdom could rescue its people from me or my ancestors. What chance does your God have of rescuing you from me?”
Sennacherib’s officials kept talking against the LORD God and his servant Hezekiah.
Sennacherib also sent letters insulting the LORD, the God of Israel. He wrote, “The gods of the other nations couldn’t save their people from me. Hezekiah’s God won’t save his people from me either.”
They shouted in the language of the Jews to the people on Jerusalem’s wall. They wanted to frighten and rattle them so they could take the city.
They talked about the God of Jerusalem like he was one of the gods of the other peoples of the earth, things people made with their own hands.
So King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz prayed and cried out to heaven.

The LORD sent an angel who wiped out the mighty warriors, leaders, and commanders in the Assyrian king’s camp. The king went home humiliated. When he went into his god’s temple, some of his own children killed him there with a sword.
That’s how the LORD saved Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem from King Sennacherib of Assyria and from everyone else who threatened them. He guided them on every side.
Many people brought gifts to the LORD in Jerusalem and valuables to King Hezekiah of Judah. From then on, all the nations held him in high regard.
Around that time, Hezekiah got so sick he was about to die. He prayed to the LORD, who spoke to him and gave him a sign.
But Hezekiah got proud and didn’t respond as he should have to the kindness shown to him. So wrath came on him, Judah, and Jerusalem.
Then Hezekiah humbled himself over his pride, and the people of Jerusalem humbled themselves too. So the LORD’s wrath didn’t come on them during Hezekiah’s lifetime.
Hezekiah had tremendous wealth and honor. He made treasuries for his silver, gold, gems, spices, shields, and every kind of valuable vessel.
He also built storehouses for the grain, new wine, and oil, stalls for all kinds of animals, and pens for his flocks.
He acquired cities for himself and had plenty of flocks and herds, because God had given him so much.
It was Hezekiah who blocked the upper spring of Gihon and channeled the water straight down the west side of David’s city. He succeeded in everything he took on.
When officials from Babylon sent ambassadors to ask about the wonder that had happened in the land, God left Hezekiah on his own to test him and find out everything in his heart.
The rest of Hezekiah’s acts and the good things he did are recorded in the vision of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz, in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.

Hezekiah died and joined his ancestors. They buried him on the slope leading up to the tombs of David’s descendants. All Judah and the people of Jerusalem honored him when he died. His son Manasseh became king in his place.
